levels.title: Define a Useful Business KPI
levels.objective: Separate operational outcomes from attention or vanity metrics.
levels.teaching: Choose metrics that answer a real business question. A sales KPI may be order completion or average order value, not merely the number of page views.

challenges.prompt: A shop needs to know whether customers receive their paid orders. Which measure best answers that question?
challenges.feedback: Paid-order delivery rate measures fulfillment outcomes directly.

challenges.prompt: Out of 100 paid orders, 5 were refunded. What refund-rate KPI should the weekly report display?
challenges.feedback: Five divided by 100 equals 0.05, or five percent. Always show the denominator and period.

challenges.prompt: A rise in profile views proves that more customers completed purchases.
challenges.feedback: Views are activity, not completed sales; conversion or order evidence is needed.

levels.title: Summarize Data by Category
levels.objective: Group transaction records and compare meaningful subtotals.
levels.teaching: Category summaries group records by a consistent label and aggregate numeric values. Check that categories are mutually understandable before comparing.

challenges.prompt: The sheet has Tea PKR 200, Coffee 500, Tea 300, Coffee 100. Which category totals are correct?
challenges.feedback: Tea sums to 200+300=500, while Coffee sums to 500+100=600.

challenges.prompt: A pivot table lists Tea, tea, and TEA as separate items. What should you do before reporting category totals?

options.a: Treat each spelling as a new product line
options.b: Normalize the category labels against an agreed list

challenges.feedback: Consistent classification prevents one category being split into several artificial groups.

challenges.prompt: A category subtotal table should count the same transaction twice if it has a repeated category label.
challenges.feedback: Each source transaction should contribute once to its intended category; repeated labels do not imply duplicate purchases.

levels.title: Select the Right Chart
levels.objective: Choose charts that match comparison, time trend and composition tasks.
levels.teaching: Chart choice depends on the question. A line chart usually suits change over time; a bar chart compares categories. Label axes and units.

challenges.prompt: Your manager wants to see monthly orders from January through June. Which display best shows the time trend?

options.a: Line chart with months in chronological order
options.b: Pie chart with a slice for every order ID
options.c: An unlabeled image of the store

challenges.feedback: A chronological line allows readers to follow rises and falls across months.

challenges.prompt: You need to compare sales totals across four product categories in one month. Which design is clearest?

options.b: A bar chart with product names and PKR axis units
options.c: A line chart with order IDs sorted alphabetically

challenges.feedback: A labeled bar chart supports direct comparison across discrete categories.

challenges.prompt: A chart with no labels or units can still be considered a fully interpretable business report.
challenges.feedback: Readers need category/time labels and meaningful units to understand the values.

levels.title: Use Conditional Formatting Meaningfully
levels.objective: Highlight overdue transactions while preserving accessibility.
levels.teaching: Conditional formatting applies a repeatable rule to a range. Combine colors with text or symbols so important meaning is not color-only.

challenges.prompt: Orders older than seven days are overdue. Which formatting condition correctly highlights them?
challenges.feedback: A strictly greater-than-seven rule highlights days eight and above.

challenges.prompt: Your overdue rows appear only red, with no other indication. How should you make the tracker easier to use for color-blind readers?

options.b: Add a labeled Overdue status or icon alongside the visual highlight
options.c: Use two nearly identical red shades

challenges.feedback: An explicit status label communicates the rule without requiring color perception.

challenges.prompt: Under a Days Open > 7 overdue rule, an order at exactly seven days should be flagged overdue.
challenges.feedback: Seven is not greater than seven; review thresholds carefully.

levels.title: Avoid Misleading Dashboards
levels.objective: Explain how axes, selective periods and missing denominators distort interpretations.
levels.teaching: A small difference may look enormous if an axis begins near the observed values. Compare charts on fair scales and state the period and denominator.

challenges.prompt: Sales increased from PKR 98,000 to 100,000. Which axis choice risks making this modest change look dramatic?

options.a: A vertical axis starting at 97,000 without clear context
options.b: A clearly labeled zero-baseline bar chart
options.c: A table displaying both exact amounts

challenges.feedback: Truncating the vertical axis magnifies the apparent bar-height difference; the actual increase is about two percent.

challenges.prompt: A report says complaints doubled from 1 to 2 but hides that 10,000 orders were delivered. What should be added?

options.a: The order denominator and comparison period
options.b: Only a larger red complaint icon

challenges.feedback: Absolute counts need volume and timing context; two complaints among 10,000 orders differ from two among ten.

challenges.prompt: Using a consistent zero baseline for bar length comparisons makes large-looking differences less likely to mislead.
challenges.feedback: A zero baseline keeps bar-height comparisons proportional to absolute values.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Create a Simple Sales Summary
levels.objective: Interpret three monthly totals and identify limits in a summary.
levels.teaching: A useful dashboard reports verified values, change direction and limitations. Avoid causal conclusions without evidence.

challenges.prompt: Sales totals are April PKR 120,000, May 135,000, June 130,000. Which month had the highest total?
challenges.feedback: May was 135,000, above both April and June.

challenges.prompt: You want to explain the May-to-June change. What is a defensible statement?

options.a: Sales fell PKR 5,000, but these totals alone do not explain why
options.b: Customers disliked the new logo, so sales fell
options.c: Sales grew by PKR 15,000 because July was stronger

challenges.feedback: June is 5,000 below May. Cause needs additional data; don't invent reasons.

challenges.prompt: The three monthly totals alone are enough to prove that advertising caused the increase in May.
challenges.feedback: A monthly revenue pattern cannot establish the effect of one campaign without appropriate controls and attribution.
